**“Tonight I can write the saddest lines.”**  
This is the opening line of the famous poem from Neruda’s epic work *Canto General*, often quoted in quizbowl to signal the poet.

**“In you everything sank!”**  
A recurring refrain that appears in the final poem of *Twenty Love Poems and a Song of Despair* and in later collections, marking Neruda’s signature lyrical motif.

**Twenty Love Poems and a Song of Despair**  
Neruda’s first major published book (1924), a collection of love poems that established his fame; frequently mentioned as a defining work.

**Canto General**  
Neruda’s sweeping, multi‑volume historical poem about the Americas; the title itself and its sections (e.g., “The Heights of Machu Picchu”) are common clues.

**“Walking Around”**  
A well‑known poem from the *Residencia en la tierra* (1935) collection, noted for the line “I am sick of being a man.” It is a staple clue for Neruda’s existential verse.

**Elemental Odes (Odas elementales)**  
A series of short odes to everyday objects (onion, tomato, artichoke, tuna, socks, etc.) that showcase Neruda’s celebration of the mundane; often referenced by title.

**“Ode to the Onion”**  
One of the most quoted odes, famous for the line about the onion making us “cry without hurting us.” It typifies Neruda’s elemental odes.

**“Ode to My Socks”** (or “Ode to the Sock”)  
A humorous ode that includes the line “what is good is doubly good,” frequently cited as an example of Neruda’s playful object poetry.

**“The Heights of Machu Picchu”**  
A major section of *Canto General* that begins with “Arise to birth with me, my brother,” often used to link Neruda to his Latin‑American historical themes.

**“The White Bee”**  
A poem from the *Elemental Odes* collection that mentions a bee “drunk with honey,” another distinctive image tied to Neruda’s nature verses.

**“United Fruit Company”**  
A politically charged poem criticizing imperialist exploitation; the title and its reference to the fruit corporation are characteristic of Neruda’s activist side.

**“Ode to Conger Chowder”**  
An obscure but memorable ode to a specific soup, illustrating Neruda’s penchant for celebrating specific foods; appears in the *Elemental Odes*.

**“Arise to birth with me, my brother.”**  
A rallying line from “The Heights of Machu Picchu” that signals Neruda’s call for Latin‑American solidarity and is often quoted verbatim.

**“Ode to a Large Tuna in the Market.”**  
Another vivid food ode from the *Elemental Odes*, showcasing Neruda’s ability to elevate ordinary market items to poetic grandeur.
